title: Strings and Text Processing
goal: Work with std::string confidently: build, search, slice, compare and transform text.

topics.title: std::string owns its characters
topics.body: `std::string` manages its own buffer, so it can grow with `+=` and reports its length with `size()`. A C-style `char[]` does neither.

topics.title: find and substr
topics.body: `find` returns the position of a substring or `npos`. `substr(pos, len)` returns a new string, so the original is untouched.

topics.title: Transform every character
topics.body: A range-based loop over `char&` edits the string in place. `std::toupper` needs the character cast to unsigned char to be safe on all inputs.

interviewBank.answer: It owns and resizes its buffer, knows its length, supports value semantics and cannot silently overflow the way a fixed array can. A `char[]` remains useful only at API boundaries or for fixed binary data.
It is the constant returned by `find` when nothing matched. Because it is the largest possible position value, comparing against it is the correct test instead of comparing with -1.

defenseBank.q: How do you reverse a string without copying it twice?
defenseBank.answer: Swap from both ends inward, or use `std::reverse` on its iterators. Both work in place, so the cost is a linear pass with no second buffer.
steps: Name the two indices that move toward each other.
State the loop condition i < j.
Swap and advance both ends.

defenseBank.q: Why does case handling need a cast to unsigned char?
defenseBank.answer: `std::toupper` and friends require a value representable as unsigned char or EOF; a negative signed char is undefined behaviour. The cast is a correctness fix, not a style choice.

title: Pointers and References
goal: Understand addresses, dereference safely, and choose between a pointer, a reference and a value.

topics.title: Address and dereference
topics.body: `&x` yields the address of x, and `*p` reads the value stored there. A pointer is a variable whose value is an address.

topics.title: A reference is an alias
topics.body: A reference must be bound when created and cannot be rebound. Writing through it writes to the original, which is why swap takes references.

topics.title: Pointers walk an array
topics.body: Array elements are contiguous, so `p + 1` moves to the next element. The one-past-the-end pointer is valid for comparison but must never be dereferenced.

debug.title: An integer assigned to a pointer
Dereferencing a null pointer
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null)

tasks.title: Sum through a pointer
tasks.statement: Sum the three array elements using a pointer, not indexing, and print the total.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference?
interviewBank.answer: A pointer is an object that stores an address, can be null, can be rebound and needs dereferencing. A reference is an alias bound once, cannot be null and is used with ordinary syntax. Prefer a reference when the argument must exist.

interviewBank.q: Why is dereferencing a dangling pointer undefined behaviour?
interviewBank.answer: The object it points to has ended, so the memory may be reused or unmapped. Reading or writing there has no defined result, and the program can appear to work until the allocator reuses that block.

defenseBank.q: How do you explain `*` and `&` without confusing a beginner?
defenseBank.answer: `&` asks where a variable lives, `*` asks what lives at an address. One takes the address, the other follows it, and the pair cancels when used together.
steps: Draw a box for the variable and a label for the address.
Draw an arrow from the pointer to the box.
Read `*p` aloud as the value at that arrow.

defenseBank.q: When is a raw pointer still the right parameter type?
defenseBank.answer: When null is a meaningful value or the pointer is optional and not owned. Otherwise a reference states that the object exists, and a smart pointer states who owns it.

title: Dynamic Memory and RAII
goal: Allocate and release heap memory correctly, then replace manual new/delete with smart pointers.

topics.title: new and delete
topics.body: `new` returns an address on the free store and `delete` releases it. Arrays need `new[]` with `delete[]`; mixing them is undefined behaviour.

topics.title: unique_ptr owns one object
topics.body: `std::make_unique` allocates and transfers ownership to a `unique_ptr`, which deletes the object when it goes out of scope. Copying is forbidden; moving is allowed.

topics.title: shared_ptr counts owners
topics.body: `shared_ptr` keeps a reference count and deletes the object when the last owner goes away. Use it for genuinely shared lifetime, not as a default.

debug.title: A double delete
debug.error: the program failed at runtime (exit null) — free(): double free detected in tcache 2

tasks.title: Heap array with unique_ptr
tasks.statement: Allocate three integers on the heap with make_unique<int[]>, fill them with 1, 2, 3 and print their sum.

interviewBank.answer: That a resource is released when its owning object's lifetime ends, including during stack unwinding from an exception. The destructor is the release point, so no manual cleanup path can be forgotten.

interviewBank.q: When would you choose shared_ptr over unique_ptr?
interviewBank.answer: Only when several independent owners must keep the same object alive and no single owner can define its lifetime. Exclusive ownership is simpler and cheaper, so unique_ptr is the default.

defenseBank.q: How do you find a memory leak in a small program?
defenseBank.answer: I look for every new and check for a matching delete on all paths, then run the program under AddressSanitizer, which reports the allocation that leaked.
steps: List allocation sites and their release paths.
Check early returns and exception paths.
Rebuild with -fsanitize=address and read the report.

defenseBank.q: Why is `delete p; delete p;` worse than a leak?
defenseBank.answer: A leak wastes memory but leaves the program defined. A double delete corrupts the allocator's bookkeeping, which is undefined behaviour and often crashes somewhere unrelated later.

title: Structs, Enums and Namespaces
goal: Group related data in a struct, give constants a type-safe enum, and keep names from colliding.

topics.title: A struct groups fields
topics.body: A struct is a named collection of fields with independent types. Aggregate initialization fills them in declaration order.

topics.title: enum class is scoped
topics.body: `enum class` keeps its enumerators inside the type name and does not convert to int implicitly, which prevents accidental comparisons with unrelated numbers.

topics.title: A namespace names a region
topics.body: A namespace qualifies its members, so two libraries can both define `print`. Access with `ns::name` rather than importing everything.

An enum class used as an int

tasks.title: Average marks from records
tasks.statement: Create three Student records and print their average marks as an integer.

interviewBank.q: What is the difference between a struct and a class in C++?
interviewBank.answer: The only language difference is the default access: public for a struct, private for a class, and public for inheritance from a struct. Convention uses struct for passive data and class for types with invariants.

interviewBank.q: Why prefer enum class to a plain enum?
interviewBank.answer: It is scoped, so enumerator names cannot collide, and it is strongly typed, so no implicit conversion to int. A plain enum leaks its names into the enclosing scope and converts silently.

defenseBank.q: When is a struct the wrong abstraction?
defenseBank.answer: When the fields must change together to stay valid. A struct with public fields cannot enforce that, so the invariant belongs behind a class with a constructor and private members.
steps: Name the invariant that must always hold.
Show how a public field could break it.
Move the fields behind a constructor.

defenseBank.q: Why avoid `using namespace` in a header?
defenseBank.answer: It injects every name into every file that includes the header, where unrelated code can collide with it. Qualifying names or importing a single name keeps the effect local.

title: Object-Oriented Programming Fundamentals
goal: Model a real thing as a class with private data, public behaviour and a stated invariant.

topics.title: A class owns its state
topics.body: Data members hold the state and member functions define the behaviour. Keeping the data private means every change goes through a function that can enforce the rules.

topics.title: Getters and setters with a rule
topics.body: A setter is only worth writing when it validates. Here the balance cannot go negative, so `withdraw` refuses instead of leaving the object inconsistent.

topics.title: const member functions
topics.body: A `const` member function promises not to change the object, so it callable on a const reference. Reading methods should be const; that is what makes `print(const Account&)` possible.

debug.title: A class body without its semicolon

tasks.title: A bank account class
tasks.statement: Implement Account with deposit and a withdraw that refuses to overdraw, then print the final balance.

interviewBank.answer: It is not just private fields: it is that every state change goes through an operation that preserves the object's invariant. Without the invariant, private data is only hidden, not protected.

interviewBank.q: Why does a getter exist if the field could simply be public?
interviewBank.answer: A getter keeps the representation free to change and lets the class compute the value rather than store it. It also keeps the field read-only from outside while internal code can still update it.

defenseBank.q: A teammate wants public fields to save time. How do you respond?
defenseBank.answer: Public fields are fine for a passive record with no invariant. The moment a value must stay valid, the class needs a function that can reject a bad change.
steps: Ask whether any combination of field values is invalid.
If yes, name the function that must enforce it.
Keep the fields private behind that function.

defenseBank.answer: A statement that is true of every valid object between public operations — for example, a balance is never negative. Constructors establish it and every mutator preserves it.

title: Constructors, Destructors and Class Design
goal: Initialize objects correctly, understand lifetime and destruction order, and know when the compiler-generated operations are enough.

topics.title: Constructor initialization lists
topics.body: Members are initialized in declaration order, before the body runs. An initializer list is the correct place to set them, and the order in the list cannot override declaration order.

topics.title: A destructor runs at the end of lifetime
topics.body: The destructor releases whatever the constructor acquired. For a stack object it runs at the closing brace, in reverse order of construction.

topics.title: Rule of Zero
topics.body: If a class manages no resource directly, do not write a destructor, copy or move operation: the compiler-generated ones are correct. Write them only when you own a resource.

debug.title: A constructor with a return type
debug.error: error: return type specification for constructor invalid

debug.title: Initialization order contradicts the list
debug.error: Wrong output: 6 5 — members initialize in declaration order, so second_ used an uninitialized first_.

tasks.title: A class with visible lifetime
tasks.statement: Create a class whose constructor prints open and destructor prints close; build one in main and print work between them.

interviewBank.q: What is the Rule of Three and why does it exist?
interviewBank.answer: If a class needs a custom destructor, copy constructor or copy assignment, it almost always needs all three, because they all manage the same resource. Getting one right and the others wrong gives double frees or leaks.

interviewBank.q: Why can member initialization order surprise you?
interviewBank.answer: Members are initialized in declaration order, not in the order written in the initializer list. A member that reads another must be declared after it.

defenseBank.q: How do you decide whether a destructor should be virtual?
defenseBank.answer: If the class is meant to be a polymorphic base and deletion can happen through a base pointer, the destructor must be virtual; otherwise deleting through the base is undefined behaviour.
steps: Ask whether deletion can occur through a base pointer.
If yes, make the base destructor virtual.
Keep non-polymorphic value types non-virtual.

defenseBank.q: Why is Rule of Zero the default advice?
defenseBank.answer: The compiler's copy and move operations are correct for types that own nothing directly. Writing them by hand only adds a chance to get lifetime wrong.

title: Inheritance and Composition
goal: Reuse behaviour through a base class or a member, and choose composition when inheritance would be wrong.

topics.title: Public inheritance is an is-a
topics.body: A derived class inherits the base's public interface and can add its own state. Constructors run base first, then members, then the derived body.

topics.title: Composition is a has-a
topics.body: A class can hold another object as a member. Composition keeps the two lifetimes explicit and avoids the fragile base-class coupling inheritance creates.

topics.title: protected is for derived classes
topics.body: `protected` exposes a member to derived classes but not to outside code. Use it for state a derived class genuinely needs, not as a shortcut for public fields.

interviewBank.q: Inheritance or composition: how do you decide?
interviewBank.answer: If the derived type genuinely is a kind of the base and must be usable through its interface, inheritance fits. If it merely uses the other type's behaviour, composition is safer and does not couple the two hierarchies.

Two base classes sharing a common ancestor give the most-derived object two copies of that ancestor, so a member reference is ambiguous. Virtual inheritance solves it by sharing one base subobject, at a cost in complexity.

defenseBank.q: Why can deep inheritance hierarchies become fragile?
defenseBank.answer: A change in a base class reaches every derived class, and the derived classes may depend on protected details that were never a contract. Composition keeps that dependency explicit and local.
steps: Count how many classes depend on the base's details.
Name a change that would break them.
Show the composition that would localise it.

defenseBank.q: What does the base constructor run before the derived one?
defenseBank.answer: Construction goes base first so the derived body can rely on a fully constructed base. Destruction goes the other way: derived first, then base.
